checks: Realize X as k independent unit exponential phases. These preserve two strictly positive phases, and −E_0 preserves one strictly negative phase even when residual coefficients vanish. The chain rule for c_i=−b_i gives the minus sign in the derivative formula.

Writing the added negative phase convolution as e^(x/c) times a tail integral gives f_W′=(f_W−f_U)/c for c>0. At c=0 the distributions agree, and f_W′ exists by the density sign lemma. Removing the j phase in ∂_i and the i phase in ∂_j yields −(b_i−b_j)f_W′(0).

The negative means for W have total 1+(k−1)+b_i+b_j=k+b_i+b_j, and every one lies in [0,1]. The density derivative is strictly negative for b_i+b_j>0 because its equality case has total exactly k. Along an unequal transfer pair, b_i>b_j and b_i+b_j>0 up to the terminal point. The derivative along the path is (b_i−b_j)f_W′(0)<0 before that point, so the exact endpoint is included by the mean value theorem. Continuity through b_j=0 follows from the accepted derivative lemma.

The endpoint is the smaller of the above-average excess and below-average deficit, so it keeps all coefficients in the box and fixes at least one new coordinate at the average. The sum forces an above-average and below-average pair whenever unequal. A finite sequence therefore reaches the equal vector, with strict improvement whenever it starts unequal. For q=k−1 all coordinates are already one.
